title: When something goes wrong
hook: Someone lost coins to a scam and posted about it. Minutes later they got a message: "I'm a recovery expert. I can get your coins back for a small fee."
card1: If you are scammed, act fast: stop sending, tell an adult, save screenshots and addresses, and report it to the platform and the police.
analogy1: A recovery scam is like a fake locksmith who turns up right after a burglary and offers to get your things back, if you pay first.
card2: No one can reverse a blockchain [[transaction]]. People who promise to "recover" coins for a fee are almost always scammers targeting victims a second time.
card3: Feeling embarrassed is normal, but staying quiet helps scammers. Reporting warns others, and the police collect these reports.

recovery.prompt: You lost practice coins to a fake giveaway. Now "CryptoRecoveryPro" writes: "I can trace and return your coins. Pay 10 coins for the recovery software."

pay.label: Pay 10 coins to get the rest back
pay.before: You will send 10 practice coins to the "expert".
pay.what: They asked for 20 more for "taxes", then disappeared. You lost another 10 coins.
pay.why: Recovery scammers look for people who have just lost money.
pay.how: They watch posts and comments where people talk about being scammed.
pay.realLife: Real police and platforms never charge you to look into a case.

proof.label: Ask them to prove they are real
proof.before: You will ask for proof before paying.
proof.what: They sent screenshots of "happy clients". Fake, but convincing. You haven't paid yet.
proof.why: Fake proof is easy to make. Talking to them only gives them more chances.
proof.how: Screenshots and reviews can be made up in minutes.

report.label: Block them, tell a parent and report it
report.before: You will stop the chat and get help.
report.what: Your parent helped you report the first scam to the platform and the police. The "recovery" account was reported too.
report.why: Reporting is what actually helps, and it protects other people.
report.how: The police collect reports to find patterns and catch scammers.
report.realLife: In many countries you can report a crime to the police online. Keep screenshots and addresses as evidence.

q1.prompt: Someone offers to recover your lost coins for a fee. What is it most likely to be?
q1.b: A real service that can reverse the transaction
q1.explanation: No one can reverse a blockchain transaction, and the police never charge you. It's a second scam.

q2.prompt: You have been scammed. What should you do first?
q2.b: Stop sending, tell an adult and save evidence
q2.c: Send a bit more to unlock your money
q2.explanation: Stop, tell someone you trust, keep the evidence and report it.

q3.prompt: Why report a scam if the coins can't be returned?
q3.a: It warns others and helps the police find scammers
q3.c: So that you get in trouble
q3.explanation: Reports help stop scammers and protect other people. Victims don't get in trouble for reporting.

misc.recoveryReal: "Recovery experts can reverse transactions." No one can reverse a blockchain transaction.
misc.recoveryPolice: "It's the police." The police never charge money to investigate.
misc.hideIt: "Keep it secret so no one knows." Silence helps scammers. Telling an adult gets you help.
misc.sendMore: "Send more to unlock the rest." Scammers always invent new fees.
misc.noPoint: "Reporting is pointless." Reports help stop scammers and protect others.
misc.reportBlame: "I'll get in trouble for reporting." Victims don't get in trouble for reporting a crime.

t1: If you are scammed: stop, tell an adult, save evidence, report it.
t2: No one can reverse a blockchain [[transaction]]. "Recovery for a fee" is a scam.
t3: Reporting helps others, even when the coins don't come back.
talk1: If one of us were scammed online, who would we tell first and what would we do?
talk2: Why do you think people feel embarrassed after being scammed?
